Expound
eks-POWND
v.
Latin exponere, “to set forth, explain,” from ex- (out) + ponere (to place). Renders the Greek diermeneuō, “to interpret thoroughly,” ektithemi, “to set forth,” and epiluō, “to loose, explain.”

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

📖 Biblical Definition

To expound is to open up the meaning of a text of Scripture—to lay out what is there, to make plain what is folded, to set forth the sense, scope, and application of God’s Word for the understanding of the hearer. The supreme biblical model is the risen Christ on the Emmaus road: beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself; and later in the upper room, He opened... their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures. Exposition—the verbal noun of expound—is therefore Christ’s own method of teaching: He takes the texts, He sets forth what they mean, He shows how they point to Him, He applies them to the hearer. Philip on the desert road expounds Isaiah 53 to the Ethiopian eunuch and preaches Jesus from the text. Apollos in Ephesus, having been instructed more perfectly in the way of God by Aquila and Priscilla, mightily convinces the Jews by the scriptures. Paul at Rome expounded and testified the kingdom of God, persuading them concerning Jesus, both out of the law of Moses, and out of the prophets, from morning till evening. Exposition is therefore the central element of biblical teaching: not the speaker’s thoughts illustrated occasionally by Scripture, but Scripture itself opened up so that the divine sense of the text becomes the substance of what is delivered. Faithful exposition has marks. It is grounded in the text; it follows the text’s grammar, context, and flow; it traces the text’s connection to the whole counsel of God and especially to Christ; and it presses the text’s sense home to the conscience and life of the hearer. It rejects on one side the topical sermon that uses a verse as pretext for the preacher’s opinions, and on the other the dry exegetical lecture that hands the hearer information without the application Scripture is given to produce. To expound is to set the text forth in such a way that the hearer meets, in the preacher’s voice, the voice of God speaking from His own Word.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines EXPOUND as to explain; to lay open the meaning; to clear of obscurity; to interpret; as, to expound a text of scripture, a law, a statute.

expand to see more

EXPOUND, v.t. — 1. To explain; to lay open the meaning; to clear of obscurity; to interpret; as, to expound a text of scripture, a law, a statute. 2. To lay open; to examine carefully; as, to expound one’s self.

EXPOUNDING, ppr. — Explaining; laying open the meaning; interpreting.

📖 Key Scripture

Luke 24:27 — "And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself."

Acts 8:35 — "Then Philip opened his mouth, and began at the same scripture, and preached unto him Jesus."

Acts 28:23 — "...he expounded and testified the kingdom of God, persuading them concerning Jesus, both out of the law of Moses, and out of the prophets, from morning till evening."

Nehemiah 8:8 — "So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Biblical exposition is corrupted by the topical sermon that uses a verse as a launching pad for the speaker’s opinions while the text itself is left unopened—and by the dry exegetical lecture that opens the text technically but never presses its sense home to the conscience of the hearer.

expand to see more

The most pervasive contemporary corruption of exposition is the topical sermon in which a verse is announced, briefly read, and then abandoned as the speaker moves to the actual content of his talk: cultural commentary, personal anecdote, motivational application, the speaker’s opinions on the issues of the week. The text is the pretext; the divine sense of the passage is never opened up; the hearer leaves having heard the speaker’s thoughts illustrated occasionally by Scripture rather than Scripture itself laid out and applied. Nehemiah 8:8 is the standing rebuke: so they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading. Read the text, give its sense, cause the people to understand—not deliver the speaker’s reflections garnished with Scripture, but expound the Word so that the hearer meets God in His own speech.

The opposite corruption is the dry exegetical lecture that opens the text technically—explains the Greek tense, traces the literary structure, surveys the scholarly options—but never presses the sense home to the conscience and life of the hearer. The information has been delivered; the application has not. Biblical exposition is more than analysis; it is the setting forth of the text’s sense for the hearer, with the application Scripture itself is given to produce. The risen Christ on the road to Emmaus did not merely catalogue the Old Testament texts about Himself; He expounded them so that the disciples’ hearts burned within them. Recover both ends: the substantive opening of the text (against the topical pretext) and the warm pressing of the text home (against the dry lecture), and exposition recovers its biblical shape—Christ’s own method of teaching, by which the people of God hear the voice of God in the Word of God.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek diermeneuō (to interpret thoroughly), ektithemi (to set forth), and epiluō (to loose, explain); Hebrew pārash (to make distinct, Neh 8:8)—the laying-open of the text’s sense so that the hearer meets God in His own speech.

expand to see more

Greek diermeneuō (G1329) — to interpret thoroughly, expound (Luke 24:27).

Greek ektithemi (G1620) — to set forth, expose, explain (Acts 11:4; 18:26; 28:23).

Greek epiluō (G1956) — to loose, solve, explain (Mark 4:34, “he expounded all things to his disciples”).

Hebrew pārash (H6567) — to make distinct, declare; Neh 8:8’s “gave the sense.”

Usage

"Exposition is Christ’s own method—the risen Lord on the Emmaus road expounded the Scriptures concerning Himself."

"Read the text, give its sense, cause the people to understand—Nehemiah 8:8 is the standing rebuke to the topical-sermon corruption."

"Dry exegetical lecture opens the text and leaves it cold; biblical exposition opens it and presses its sense home until the hearer’s heart burns."
